title: A Kingdom Coming Apart: Five Kings and Assyria's Shadow
summary: In Judah, Azariah (also called Uzziah) reigns a long time and does right but is struck with a skin disease, and his son Jotham governs and then succeeds him. In Israel, the dynasty of Jehu ends with Zechariah's murder, and four kings follow in quick succession, three of them by assassination: Shallum, Menahem, Pekahiah, and Pekah. Assyria enters the story, first taking tribute from Menahem and then, under Tiglath-pileser, carrying off the people of Galilee and Gilead into exile.
story: Chapter 14 ended with Jeroboam II's restored borders, a high tide of northern prosperity. This chapter shows how quickly the tide went out. Within a few years of Jeroboam's death, Israel has six months of one king, one month of another, a civil war, and an empire at the door. The word to Jehu in 10:30, that four generations of his sons would sit on the throne, is fulfilled and then exhausted. Judah, by contrast, has two long and relatively stable reigns, which sharpens the contrast between the kingdoms. For the first time the Assyrian empire takes Israelite land and deports its people, a preview of the end that comes in chapter 17. The note at verse 37, that the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah, opens the crisis of chapter 16.
historical:
Azariah reigned from about 792 to 740 BC, much of it as co-regent with his father at the start and with his son Jotham at the end; the reckoning of these overlaps is debated. Isaiah dates his call vision to the year King Uzziah died (Isaiah 6:1). Second Chronicles 26 adds that Uzziah's disease came after he entered the temple to burn incense, a task reserved for priests.

The decisive figure outside Israel is Tiglath-pileser III, who ruled Assyria from 745 to 727 BC and turned it into an empire that absorbed rather than merely raided its neighbors. The Bible calls him Pul in verse 19; Babylonian records knew him by that name, and 1 Chronicles 5:26 names both Pul and Tiglath-pileser. His own inscriptions list Menahem of Samaria among the kings who paid him tribute, usually dated around 738 BC. In about 733 to 732 BC he campaigned against Damascus and Israel, took Galilee and the lands east of the Jordan, and deported their populations. His inscriptions also claim that the Israelites overthrew Pekah and that he placed Hoshea on the throne, which fits verse 30. Excavations at Hazor, one of the cities named in verse 29, found a thick destruction layer from this period. Pekah's twenty years are hard to fit into the chronology, and many scholars think he first ruled as a rival king in Gilead before seizing Samaria.
cultural:
Menahem's tribute is a window into the economics of vassal kingship. A talent was about 3,000 shekels, so a thousand talents at fifty shekels a head means Menahem taxed roughly sixty thousand landowners. The phrase the BSB renders "wealthy men" is the same word used elsewhere for mighty warriors, which suggests the landed class who owed military service. Paying the great king bought his recognition, and verse 19 says plainly that Menahem did it to strengthen his own grip on the kingdom. Tribute of this kind protected a ruler while it drained his people.

Azariah's disease, traditionally translated leprosy, was a condition the law of Leviticus 13 and 14 called tsaraat, a term covering a range of skin diseases, not only what medicine now calls Hansen's disease. It made a person ritually unclean and required living apart from the community, which is why the king lived in a separate house and could not enter the temple. Menahem's atrocity at Tiphsah, ripping open pregnant women, was a terror tactic recorded elsewhere in the ancient Near East and denounced by the prophets (Amos 1:13 condemns the Ammonites for it). The narrator reports it without comment, but no reader of Amos could miss the judgment behind it.
literary: This is the most compressed chapter of royal formulas in Kings. Seven reigns are covered in thirty-eight verses, and the formulas themselves become the message: the same verdict ("he did evil in the sight of the LORD") falls on every northern king, and the same flight from Jeroboam's sins is never taken. The Judah sections form an outer frame (Azariah at the start, Jotham at the end) around the rapid collapse in the north. The repeated verb "conspired" and the sequence of striking down, killing, and reigning "in his place" drum through the middle like a refrain. Verse 12 is the only place the narrator pauses to interpret, tying Zechariah's death to the word spoken to Jehu. Verse 37 is set apart as a kind of forward-looking aside.

outline.t: Azariah of Judah and his disease
Zechariah: the end of Jehu's dynasty
Pekah, Tiglath-pileser, and the first deportations

doctrines.note: The chapter shows judgment working through history: a nation that will not turn from its sins is handed over to its own violence and then to a foreign power. The deportations of verse 29 are the first installment of the exile the law had warned of.

Verse 12 notes that the word of the LORD to Jehu was fulfilled exactly. Kings keeps pointing to prophecy and fulfillment to show that history is not random; God speaks, and what he says comes to pass.
Verse 37 says the LORD began to send Rezin and Pekah against Judah. Even the hostile moves of foreign kings are described as under God's direction, without excusing those kings for their own aims.

words.note: Qashar, to conspire, literally to tie or bind together. Its use four times in this chapter shows the northern kingdom tying itself in knots of plot and counterplot. The same verb described the plots against Joash and Amaziah in Judah; it is the characteristic word for a political order without legitimacy.

Tsara, to be struck with a skin disease. The verb stands behind the noun tsaraat, the condition regulated in Leviticus 13 and 14. It covered several afflictions, not only modern leprosy, and its main effect in Israel was ritual separation. The text says the LORD afflicted the king, so it reads the disease as a judgment, a point Chronicles explains further.

Galah, to uncover, reveal, or go into exile. In the form used here it means to carry people away captive. This is the first time in Kings that Israelites are deported to Assyria, and the word will return with full force in 17:6 and 25:21.

christ: The chapter speaks of Christ mainly by what it lacks. Israel has king after king, and none of them can hold the throne, restrain violence, or turn the people from their sins. The regions named in verse 29, Galilee and the land of Naphtali, are the first to go into darkness under Assyria. Isaiah picks up that loss directly in a promise: the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, humbled in the former time, would see a great light (Isaiah 9:1-2). Matthew quotes that promise when Jesus begins his ministry in Galilee, in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali (Matthew 4:12-16). The first region to fall to Assyria is the first to hear the gospel preached by the true king.

hard.q: Why does the chapter report Menahem's atrocity at Tiphsah without condemning it?
hard.a:
Kings often narrates terrible deeds without editorial comment, and some readers take this as indifference. But the book works by accumulation. Menahem receives the standard verdict that he did evil in the sight of the LORD, and his reign sits in a chapter whose whole message is that the northern kingdom is collapsing under its own violence. The prophets of the same generation say explicitly what the narrator implies. Amos names this very crime as a reason for God's judgment on Ammon, and Hosea describes Samaria's end in similar terms (Hosea 13:16).

It helps to remember that describing is not approving. The Bible records the worst of what its own people did, which is part of why its account can be trusted, and it leaves the reader to feel the horror. The silence is not neutrality; it is the silence of a narrator who expects the reader to know what God thinks of such things.

questions: Menahem paid a heavy price to secure his own position, and the people paid it for him. Where do you see leaders protecting themselves at the expense of those they serve?
Azariah was a good king who still ended his days in isolation. How do you hold together faithfulness and suffering that seems to come from God's hand?
Galilee was the first to fall into darkness and the first to see the light of Jesus. What does that pattern suggest about where God chooses to begin?
